title: Decisions in one instruction: csel, cinc, and cbz
summary: Pick one of two values with csel, count with cinc and cset, and branch on zero with cbz and cbnz, in fewer lines than cmp and b.cond need.

body.markdown:
Read these first:

- [Conditionals with cmp and b.cond](/learn/assembly-conditionals-basics)
- [Pre-test loops](/learn/pretest-loop)
- [Post-test loops](/learn/post-test-loop)

An if-else that only chooses between two values costs a `cmp`, two branches, and two labels. AArch64 has instructions that make the choice in one line after the `cmp`, and branches that test a register for zero with no `cmp` at all. This lesson covers both kinds and uses them in three short programs.

## Picking a value with csel

`csel w0, w1, w2, cond` (*conditional select*) reads the flags the same way `b.cond` does. When the condition holds, it copies `w1` into `w0`. When it does not, it copies `w2`. It never jumps. C writes the same choice with the `?:` operator:
Here is that line in assembly twice, first with branches and then with `csel`:

body.source:
// with branches: two jumps and two labels
        cmp     raw_r, 0
        b.ge    keep_raw
        mov     level_r, 0
        b       picked
keep_raw:
        mov     level_r, raw_r
picked:

        // with csel: one line after the cmp
        cmp     raw_r, 0
        csel    level_r, wzr, raw_r, lt

body.markdown:
The condition names are the ones `b.cond` uses: `lt`, `le`, `gt` and `ge` for signed values, `lo`, `ls`, `hi` and `hs` for unsigned ones, and `eq` and `ne` for both. `wzr`, the zero register, always reads as 0, so it hands `csel` a zero without using up a register. Both sources must be registers, so to choose any other constant, `mov` it into a register first.

The program below clamps each reading into the range 0 to 100, the way a volume knob stops at either end: below 0 becomes 0 and above 100 becomes 100. Two `csel` instructions do the work, so the clamp itself has no conditional branch (no `b.cond`). It prints:

body.source:
raw  -30 -> level   0
raw   15 -> level  15
raw   60 -> level  60
raw  105 -> level 100
raw  150 -> level 100

body.starter:
// Squeeze each raw reading into the range 0 to 100 with two csel
// instructions, so the clamp itself has no conditional branch (no b.cond)

define(fp, x29)
define(lr, x30)
define(raw_r, w19)
define(level_r, w20)

define(FIRST, -30)
define(LAST, 150)
define(STEP, 45)
define(TOP, 100)

.data
fmt_row:    .string "raw %4d -> level %3d\n"

.text
        .balign 4
        .global main
main:
        stp     fp, lr, [sp, -16]!
        mov     fp, sp

        mov     raw_r, FIRST
        b       clamp_test
clamp_loop:
        cmp     raw_r, 0
        csel    level_r, wzr, raw_r, lt     // below 0: take 0, else take raw
        mov     w9, TOP
        cmp     level_r, w9
        csel    level_r, w9, level_r, gt    // above 100: take 100, else keep it

        ldr     x0, =fmt_row
        mov     w1, raw_r
        mov     w2, level_r
        bl      printf

        add     raw_r, raw_r, STEP
clamp_test:
        cmp     raw_r, LAST
        b.le    clamp_loop

        mov     w0, 0
        ldp     fp, lr, [sp], 16
        ret

expectedOutput.stdout:
raw  -30 -> level   0
raw   15 -> level  15
raw   60 -> level  60
raw  105 -> level 100
raw  150 -> level 100

body.markdown: `w9` holds 100 only from its `mov` to the second `csel`, with no call in between, so a scratch register is safe there. `raw_r` and `level_r` must still hold their values after `printf`, so they live in `w19` and `w20`.

## Counting with cset and cinc

Two more instructions turn a condition into a number. `cset w0, cond` (*conditional set*) writes 1 to `w0` when the condition holds and 0 when it does not. `cinc w0, w1, cond` (*conditional increment*) writes `w1 + 1` when the condition holds and `w1` unchanged when it does not. Written as `cinc count_r, count_r, eq`, it adds one to a count only when the last compare found the two values equal:

body.source:
cmp     w0, 0
        cset    w1, lt                      // w1 = 1 when w0 is negative, else 0
        cinc    w2, w2, ge                  // one more in w2 when w0 is not negative

body.markdown: The program below counts the numbers from 1 to 100 that 3 divides, that 5 divides, and that both divide. The remainder comes from `udiv` and `msub`, as in [Arithmetic, and the missing remainder](/learn/arithmetic-instructions), and a number is divisible when its remainder is 0. For both at once, the program adds the two remainders. Neither one is ever negative, so their sum is 0 only when both are 0. It prints:

body.source: 1 to 100: 33 divisible by 3, 20 by 5, 6 by both

body.starter:
// Count the numbers from 1 to 100 that 3 divides, that 5 divides, and that
// both divide, with one cinc per count and no branch inside the loop

define(fp, x29)
define(lr, x30)
define(n_r, w19)
define(by3_r, w20)
define(by5_r, w21)
define(both_r, w22)

define(LAST, 100)

.data
fmt_out:    .string "1 to %d: %d divisible by 3, %d by 5, %d by both\n"

.text
        .balign 4
        .global main
main:
        stp     fp, lr, [sp, -16]!
        mov     fp, sp

        mov     by3_r, 0
        mov     by5_r, 0
        mov     both_r, 0
        mov     w12, 3                      // the divisors stay in registers:
        mov     w13, 5                      // udiv and msub take no immediates

        mov     n_r, 1
        b       count_test
count_loop:
        udiv    w9, n_r, w12
        msub    w9, w9, w12, n_r            // w9 = n % 3
        udiv    w10, n_r, w13
        msub    w10, w10, w13, n_r          // w10 = n % 5

        cmp     w9, 0
        cinc    by3_r, by3_r, eq            // one more when n % 3 is 0
        cmp     w10, 0
        cinc    by5_r, by5_r, eq            // one more when n % 5 is 0
        add     w11, w9, w10                // two remainders that are never negative
        cmp     w11, 0                      // add to 0 only when both are 0
        cinc    both_r, both_r, eq

        add     n_r, n_r, 1
count_test:
        cmp     n_r, LAST
        b.le    count_loop

        ldr     x0, =fmt_out
        mov     w1, LAST
        mov     w2, by3_r
        mov     w3, by5_r
        mov     w4, both_r
        bl      printf

        mov     w0, 0
        ldp     fp, lr, [sp], 16
        ret

expectedOutput.stdout: 1 to 100: 33 divisible by 3, 20 by 5, 6 by both

body.markdown: `cset` and `cinc` are other names for `csinc` (*conditional select increment*), which gives its first source when the condition holds and its second source plus 1 when it does not. `cinc w0, w1, eq` is `csinc w0, w1, w1, ne`, with the condition turned around, so a disassembler may show you the `csinc` form.

## Branching on zero with cbz and cbnz

Testing a register against 0 is common enough to have its own branches. `cbz w19, label` (*compare and branch on zero*) jumps when `w19` is 0, and `cbnz w19, label` jumps when it is not. Each one does the work of a `cmp w19, 0` followed by `b.eq` or `b.ne`, in one instruction.

The countdown below uses both. The `cbz` before the loop skips the loop when the count starts at 0, the job the jump to the test does in a pre-test loop. The `cbnz` at the bottom sends it round again until the count reaches 0. It prints:

body.starter:
// Count down to liftoff: cbz and cbnz test the counter for zero
// without a cmp in front of them

define(fp, x29)
define(lr, x30)
define(count_r, w19)

define(START, 5)                                // try 0 too

.data
fmt_tick:   .string "%d...\n"
fmt_go:     .string "liftoff\n"

.text
        .balign 4
        .global main
main:
        stp     fp, lr, [sp, -16]!
        mov     fp, sp

        mov     count_r, START
        cbz     count_r, launch             // a start of 0 skips the countdown
tick:
        ldr     x0, =fmt_tick
        mov     w1, count_r
        bl      printf
        sub     count_r, count_r, 1         // sub leaves the flags alone
        cbnz    count_r, tick               // go again until the count reaches 0
launch:
        ldr     x0, =fmt_go
        bl      printf

        mov     w0, 0
        ldp     fp, lr, [sp], 16
        ret

body.markdown: Set `START` to 0 and the program prints only `liftoff`: the `cbz` jumps straight past the loop.

`cbz` and `cbnz` compare with 0 and nothing else; to stop at 10, use `cmp` and `b.cond`. They also leave the flags alone, so a `b.eq` after a `cbz` reads whatever the last `cmp` left behind, not the result of the `cbz`.

[tbz](/reference#tbz) and [tbnz](/reference#tbnz) do the same job for a single bit: they jump when the bit you name is 0, or when it is 1. Every instruction in this lesson has a reference entry with an example to run: [csel](/reference#csel), [cset](/reference#cset), [cinc](/reference#cinc), [csinc](/reference#csinc), [cbz](/reference#cbz) and [cbnz](/reference#cbnz).

## Check yourself

1. After `cmp w1, w2`, which one instruction puts the smaller of the two in `w0`, reading both as signed?
2. After `cmp w3, w3`, what do `cset w4, eq` and `cset w5, ne` leave in `w4` and `w5`?
3. `w6` holds 7. What does it hold after `cmp w6, 10` and then `cinc w6, w6, gt`?
4. Which one instruction does the work of `cmp w19, 0` followed by `b.ne again`?
5. In the clamp program, the first `csel` gets its 0 from `wzr`. Why does the second one need `w9`?

Answers:

1. `csel w0, w1, w2, lt`. With `le` it also works: when the two are equal, either one is the smaller.
2. `w4` holds 1 and `w5` holds 0. The values are equal, so the compare set Z.
3. 7. The condition 7 > 10 is false, so `cinc` leaves the value as it was.
4. `cbnz w19, again`.
5. `csel` chooses between two registers. `wzr` always reads as 0, but no register always reads as 100, so the program puts 100 in `w9` first.
